## Trusted accounting support for attorneys and law practices

Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has worked with attorneys since 2005, when the firm opened its doors in Stillwater, Minnesota. Today the firm serves law practices across Minnesota and Wisconsin, plus clients nationwide who want a CPA already familiar with legal practice financials.

Search "accounting for law firms near me" and most results lead to generalists who handle bookkeeping for restaurants, retail shops, and law offices with the same playbook. Attorneys need something more specific: trust accounting rules, cash flow that swings with case timelines, and partner compensation structures that don't fit a standard small-business template. That's the daily work here, not an occasional specialty.

Firms across [industries](/industries), from dentists to architects, bring similar expense management concerns, but law practices carry their own compliance weight. Attorneys who work with Slachta get a team that recognizes the difference.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: law-firm-financial-review.jpg | alt: "Attorney and accountant reviewing financial reports at a law office desk" | query: "attorney reviewing documents office meeting" -->
## Financial challenges unique to running a law practice

Running a law practice comes with financial pressure points that don't show up in a typical small-business accounting engagement.

- Trust accounting requirements that demand strict separation of client funds from operating funds, with reconciliation that can't slip
- Cash flow that rises and falls with case timelines, contingency fee settlements, and retainer billing cycles
- Partner compensation structures, including origination credit, seniority tiers, and profit-sharing formulas that complicate monthly reporting
- Expense management across matters, support staff, and overhead that needs to stay visible to every partner, not just the managing partner
- Budgeting for growth, whether that means adding an associate, opening a second office, or covering a partner's retirement buyout

These aren't hypothetical concerns. They're the reason firms bring in a CPA who has already built the reporting and cash flow systems that answer them.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: outsourced-bookkeeping-law-firm.jpg | alt: "Accountant preparing monthly financial reports for a law firm client" | query: "accountant working laptop financial reports" -->
## Outsourced accounting and bookkeeping for attorneys

Monthly bookkeeping for a law firm looks different from bookkeeping for a retail business. Matter-based expense tracking matters here: costs need to trace back to the case or client they support, not just sit in a general ledger. [Outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) services from Slachta build that structure into the books from month one.

Partners get financial reports that show more than revenue and expenses. Cash flow projections account for the gap between billing a matter and collecting on it. Trust account activity stays reconciled and separate from operating funds, the way state bar rules require. When a partner asks how the firm is doing compared to last quarter, the answer is ready before the meeting starts, not scrambled together the night before.

This is the same discipline Slachta brings to [service-based businesses](/industries/service-based-businesses) generally, adjusted for the compliance realities specific to legal practice.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: law-firm-payroll-team.jpg | alt: "Payroll administrator processing paychecks for law firm staff" | query: "payroll administrator office computer" -->
## Payroll services built for law firm teams

Attorneys, paralegals, legal assistants, and office staff often sit on different pay structures inside the same firm: salaried associates, hourly paralegals, and partners who draw rather than take a paycheck. [Payroll services](/services/payroll-services) from Slachta handle that mix without creating extra work for whoever's managing HR on top of casework.

Payroll runs on schedule, tax withholdings stay accurate, and new hires get set up correctly the first time, whether the firm has three employees or thirty. Firms scaling from a solo practice to a multi-attorney office lean on this most, since adding staff shouldn't mean adding payroll headaches. Compliance stays consistent as the team grows, so nobody's guessing at year-end.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: law-firm-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA discussing tax strategy with law firm partners in conference room" | query: "business tax planning meeting professionals" -->
## Tax preparation and planning for law firms

Law firm tax preparation involves more than filing a return once a year. Entity structure decisions, whether the firm is organized as an LLC, partnership, or professional corporation, affect how partners are taxed on distributions and how much flexibility the firm has for retirement contributions and deductions.

[Business tax services](/what-we-do/tax-plus) from Slachta start with that structure question and build a plan around it. Quarterly estimates get calculated with real numbers, not guesses carried over from last year. Partners see tax strategy discussed before December, when there's still time to act on it, rather than after the year closes when options are gone.

Firms that have grown, added partners, or opened a second location get particular attention here, since those changes often shift what the right entity structure and tax approach should be going forward.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: law-partners-retirement-planning.jpg | alt: "Law firm partners meeting with advisor about retirement plan options" | query: "business partners financial planning discussion" -->
## Retirement plans and long-term financial guidance for partners

Partners at established firms often ask the same question: is the firm's retirement plan still the right one, and is it coordinated with what each partner's financial advisor already recommends? [Advisory services](/what-we-do/advisory-services) from Slachta include retirement plan evaluation as a regular part of the relationship, not a one-time project.

That means checking plan design against the firm's current partner mix, comparing contribution limits to what partners actually want to save, and staying in contact with each partner's outside financial advisor so the numbers line up. For a firm with partners at different career stages, some building toward retirement and others years from thinking about it, that coordination keeps the plan useful for everyone at the table.

## Accounting support made for independent agents and agency owners

Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has worked with insurance agencies since opening its doors in Stillwater, Minnesota, in 2005. Independent agents and agency owners across Minnesota and Wisconsin, plus clients nationwide, come to us because commission-based revenue doesn't fit neatly into standard bookkeeping templates.

We understand renewal cycles, contingent commissions, and the lag between writing a policy and seeing that revenue land in the bank account. That knowledge shapes how we set up your books, track profitability by line of business, and help you plan cash flow around a compensation structure that swings with carrier payout schedules.

Whether you run a two-person agency near Stillwater or a multi-location operation with producers across state lines, your accounting should keep pace with how your agency actually earns money.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: insurance-agent-cash-flow-review.jpg | alt: "Insurance agent reviewing commission statements and cash flow charts" | query: "insurance agent reviewing paperwork desk" -->
## Common financial challenges facing insurance agencies

Most agency owners we talk to are managing the same handful of problems, just at different scales. Commission income doesn't arrive on a predictable schedule, and books that treat it like a regular paycheck end up misleading owners about how the agency is actually performing.

- Renewal-driven revenue that spikes and dips depending on policy cycles, not calendar quarters
- Expense creep across E&O premiums, licensing fees, CRM and quoting software, and marketing spend that's rarely tracked against production
- Budgeting for growth, whether that's hiring a new producer or opening a second location, without a clear read on next quarter's cash position
- Contingent and override commissions that arrive months after the policy was written, making short-term cash flow hard to forecast

Without a system built around these patterns, owners end up guessing at profitability instead of planning around it.

<!-- block: service-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Outsourced accounting and bookkeeping for your agency

Outsourced accounting means your books get done by people who already know how insurance agencies work, without the cost of a full-time controller. We handle the ongoing bookkeeping, close your books monthly, and hand you reporting that answers the question owners actually ask: which lines of business are making money.

### Bookkeeping built for commission revenue
icon: Receipt

We reconcile commission statements against carrier deposits and categorize income by line of business, so your books reflect how your agency really earns, not a generic chart of accounts.

### Financial reporting by book of business
icon: ChartBar

Monthly financials broken out by product line and producer let you see which parts of the agency are growing and which are quietly draining resources.

### KPI tracking and profitability analysis
icon: Target

We track the metrics that matter for agencies, retention rate, revenue per producer, and expense ratio, so decisions about staffing and growth are based on numbers instead of instinct.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: insurance-agency-payroll-processing.jpg | alt: "Agency staff member processing payroll on a laptop in an office" | query: "office worker processing payroll laptop" -->
## Payroll processing for agency staff and producers

Agency payroll rarely looks like a simple salary run. You've likely got a mix of salaried support staff, hourly CSRs, and producers paid on commission splits or draws against future earnings. Getting that wrong isn't just an accounting headache, it's a compliance risk.

We manage payroll for both sides of that equation: consistent, compliant runs for salaried and hourly staff, and accurate tracking of commission draws, splits, and true-ups for your producers. Tax withholding, filings, and year-end reporting are handled on schedule, so you're not reconstructing producer compensation history every January.

If your agency adds or loses producers mid-year, we update the payroll setup as it happens instead of catching it during tax season.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: insurance-agency-tax-planning-session.jpg | alt: "Accountant and insurance agency owner discussing tax documents at a desk" | query: "accountant client tax planning meeting" -->
## Business tax planning and preparation for insurance agencies

Tax preparation is the last step, not the strategy. We plan for your agency's tax position throughout the year, looking at entity structure, quarterly estimates, and timing of income and expenses so April doesn't bring surprises.

Entity structure matters more for agencies than owners often realize. Whether your agency is set up as an S corp, LLC, or something else affects self-employment tax, how owner compensation is handled, and what deductions are available. We review that structure as your agency grows, not just at formation.

We also evaluate retirement plan options as part of tax planning, since contributions to a SEP IRA, SIMPLE IRA, or 401(k) can meaningfully reduce an owner's tax burden while building long-term savings. Preparation and filing follow directly from that planning work, so your return reflects decisions made months earlier, not last-minute adjustments.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: insurance-agency-retirement-planning-discussion.jpg | alt: "Agency owner and advisor discussing retirement plan documents together" | query: "financial advisor retirement planning discussion" -->
## Retirement planning and financial advisor collaboration

Many agency owners already work with a financial advisor on personal investments and retirement goals. We don't replace that relationship, we make it more useful. When you're evaluating a SEP IRA versus a 401(k), or deciding how much to contribute in a strong commission year, we coordinate directly with your advisor so the tax and financial planning sides line up.

That collaboration matters most for established agency owners weighing an exit, a partner buyout, or a shift toward semi-retirement. Retirement plan evaluation, cash flow projections, and personal tax planning need to move together, not in separate conversations with people who never talk to each other.

## Accounting support built for business owners who want clarity, not just compliance

Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services opened its doors in Stillwater, Minnesota, in 2005. Two decades later, the firm still works from the same premise: a tax return once a year tells you almost nothing about how your business is actually doing. Business owners need numbers they can act on in March, June, and October, not just April.

Clients come to us from Stillwater, across the Twin Cities, and from businesses scattered through Minnesota, Wisconsin, and beyond. Geography matters less than the relationship. Dentists, service-based businesses, attorneys, and architects who work with our firm get monthly visibility into cash flow, help building a real budget, and a CPA who already understands their industry before the first meeting starts. That's the difference between a preparer and an advisor.

## Specialized experience with dentists, service businesses, and growing companies

General accounting advice rarely fits a specific business well. A dental practice's overhead structure has little in common with an insurance agency's commission cycle, and a law firm's trust accounting rules don't apply to an architecture firm managing project-based revenue. Our client base concentrates in a handful of industries where we've built real depth.

### Dentists
icon: Stethoscope

Practice owners face equipment financing, associate buy-ins, and staff payroll that swings with patient volume. We help dental clients track production against overhead and plan around the cash flow gaps that come with insurance reimbursement timing.

### Service-based businesses
icon: Briefcase

Consultants, contractors, and agencies live or die by utilization and receivables. We build reporting around the KPIs that actually predict a service business's health, not generic financial statements.

### Entrepreneurs and established small businesses
icon: TrendingUp

Whether a company is three years old or thirty, growth changes what the books need to tell you. We help owners set budgets that match their stage and revisit them as the business scales.

### Insurance agencies
icon: ShieldCheck

Commission timing and carrier reconciliation create cash flow patterns that don't look like a typical business. We've worked inside those patterns long enough to plan around them.

### Attorneys and architects
icon: Scale

Most small businesses we talk to have the same short list of worries: where the cash is going, whether the budget still makes sense, and which numbers actually matter month to month. Our core services are built to answer those questions on a regular schedule, not once a year.

### Outsourced accounting
icon: Calculator

icon: Users

icon: FileCheck

## Retirement plan reviews and financial planning, coordinated with your advisor

A lot of small business owners have a financial advisor for personal investments and a CPA for taxes, and the two rarely talk to each other. That gap costs money. That might mean evaluating whether a SIMPLE IRA still fits a growing practice or whether a 401(k) with profit sharing makes more sense at the next revenue level. It might mean coordinating year-end moves with a client's financial advisor so a distribution doesn't create a tax surprise. Either way, we work alongside the advisor already in the picture rather than asking a client to choose between us.

## Make a payment

Paying your bill shouldn't require a phone call or a hunt through old emails. Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services keeps it simple: open the secure client payment portal, enter your invoice details, and confirm. Most card payments post within one business day, and you'll get an email receipt the moment the transaction clears. Returning clients can save a payment method for faster checkout next time. New here? You can pay a one-time invoice without creating an account at all.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: online-payment-methods.jpg | alt: "Person entering credit card details on a laptop for an online payment" | query: "person paying bill online laptop" -->
## Accepted payment methods

We accept the payment methods most business owners already use day to day:

- Credit and debit card (Visa, Mastercard, Discover, American Express)
- ACH bank transfer directly from your checking or savings account
- Paper check mailed to our Stillwater, Minnesota office

Card payments typically post within one business day. ACH transfers usually take two to three business days to clear, since they route through the banking network rather than a card processor. A small processing fee applies to card payments, and the portal discloses the exact amount before you confirm. ACH transfers and mailed checks carry no added fee. Choose whichever method fits your cash flow.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: invoice-details-checklist.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing an invoice and account details before paying" | query: "person reviewing invoice paperwork desk" -->
## What to have ready before you pay

Before you head to the portal, gather a few details so your payment matches the right account on the first try:

- Your invoice number, printed in the top corner of the bill we sent
- The billing name on your account, individual or business
- The exact amount due, including any partial payment you're making
- Your card number, or your bank routing and account number for ACH

Having these on hand removes the guesswork and prevents delays caused by a mismatched account name or a transposed digit. If anything on your invoice looks unfamiliar, reach out before you pay rather than after. We would rather clarify a line item up front than process a refund later.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: billing-question-call.jpg | alt: "Accountant on a phone call helping a client with a billing question" | query: "office phone call client support" -->
## Questions about your invoice or bill

Billing questions come up, especially when your invoice combines more than one engagement, like payroll processing and a quarterly tax review on the same statement. If a charge doesn't match what you expected, or you need to spread a larger balance across two or three payments, [contact our office directly](/contact) rather than guessing at the portal. We check every discrepancy against your engagement letter and prior invoices before we respond, so you get a real answer instead of a form-letter apology. Payment plan requests are handled case by case, based on the size of the invoice and your account history with us.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Security and privacy of your payment

Your payment information is encrypted the moment you enter it, and our office never sees or stores your full card or bank account number. The processor behind our payment portal meets PCI-DSS standards, the same benchmark banks and major retailers use to handle card transactions. We use your billing details only to apply your payment to the correct account and send a receipt, nothing more. If you'd rather skip entering payment details online, a check mailed to our Stillwater office works just as well.

## Resources

### Your Time Is Priceless, But the IRS Won't Deduct It: What You Can Write Off for Volunteering
URL: /resources/your-time-is-priceless-but-the-irs-wont-deduct-it-what-you-c

Every December, someone at a nonprofit board meeting in Stillwater says it out loud: "I should get some kind of tax break for all these hours." It's a reasonable thing to think. It's also wrong. The IRS draws a hard line between the value of your time and the money you actually spend doing the work, and that line trips up a lot of otherwise careful taxpayers, including business owners who serve on hospital foundations, bar association committees, or school boards alongside running their own practice.

Here's the short version: your hours are worth nothing to the IRS, no matter your hourly rate as a dentist, attorney, or architect. Your gas money, parking fees, and that uniform you had to buy for the food shelf shift? Often deductible, if you follow the rules and keep the paperwork.

## Your hours have no tax value, and that surprises people

[IRS Publication 526](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p526) is blunt about this: you cannot deduct the value of your time or services, even if you can prove exactly what that time is worth. An attorney who donates 20 hours drafting bylaws for a local nonprofit can't deduct her $400 hourly rate times 20. A dentist who spends a Saturday providing free cleanings at a community clinic can't deduct what those procedures would have billed at. Lost income while volunteering doesn't count either, so if you took unpaid leave to build houses for a week, that lost paycheck isn't a charitable deduction.

This rule catches high-earning professionals more than anyone else, because the gap between "what my time is worth" and "what I actually spent" feels enormous. It's still zero on one side of that equation.

## What you can actually write off

The deductible side of volunteering is real, just narrower than people expect. Under Publication 526, you can deduct unreimbursed out-of-pocket expenses that are directly connected with the services you give to a qualified organization, as long as they aren't personal, living, or family expenses, and the organization hasn't reimbursed you.

Common examples that hold up:

- Supplies you buy and use directly for the volunteer work, like paint for a mural project or ingredients for a fundraiser you're cooking for
- The cost of a required uniform that isn't suitable for everyday wear, plus the cost of cleaning it
- Phone calls, postage, and printing done specifically for the organization's work
- Reasonable travel expenses, including transportation, lodging, and meals, when you're away from home performing services and there's no significant element of personal vacation involved

That last one matters for board members who travel to a national conference for their nonprofit. If the trip is genuinely for the organization's work and not a vacation with a meeting bolted on, those costs can be deductible. If you extend the trip by four days to see family or sightsee, only the portion tied to the actual volunteer work counts.

## The mileage rule everyone gets wrong

Mileage driven for charitable purposes is deductible at 14 cents per mile. That rate hasn't moved since 1997, and it's set by statute rather than adjusted annually the way the business mileage rate is. Compare that to the business standard mileage rate, which sits well above 60 cents per mile in recent years, and you can see why volunteers who drive a lot for a cause feel shortchanged. It's still money back, and if you're logging regular trips to deliver meals, transport clients, or chair committee meetings across the year, 14 cents a mile adds up.

You have a choice: use the 14-cents-per-mile rate, or track your actual gas and oil costs for those specific trips. You cannot include depreciation, insurance, repairs, or general maintenance in that calculation, the way you might for a business vehicle. If you're weighing how vehicle costs factor into your broader tax picture, our piece on [leasing versus buying a car](/resources/auto-leasing-vs-buying-which-makes-more-sense) covers the business side of that math.

Whatever method you choose, keep a log: date, destination, purpose, and miles driven. "Various nonprofit trips, 2024" won't survive a records request.

## What doesn't count, no matter how good the cause

A few categories trip people up every year:

| Expense | Deductible? |
|---|---|
| Value of your time or professional services | No |
| Income lost while volunteering | No |
| Cost of a raffle, bingo, or lottery ticket, even from a qualified charity | No |
| Value of blood donated | No |
| Depreciation, insurance, or repairs on a car used for volunteer driving | No |
| Babysitting costs so you can volunteer | No |
| Required uniform not suitable for everyday use | Yes |
| Unreimbursed supplies bought specifically for the volunteer work | Yes |
| Gas and oil, or 14 cents per mile, for volunteer driving | Yes |
| Travel expenses for a trip with no significant personal vacation element | Yes |

The theme running through the "no" column is personal benefit or unproven value. The theme in the "yes" column is documented, out-of-pocket, and directly tied to the organization's work.

## Keeping records that will hold up

Two practical limits catch people off guard. First, you can only claim these deductions if you itemize on Schedule A. Given how high the standard deduction runs for most filers now, plenty of volunteers spend real money on a cause and get zero tax benefit because they're better off taking the standard deduction anyway. That's not a reason to stop tracking expenses, but it's a reason not to assume a deduction is coming.

Second, if your unreimbursed expenses for a single organization add up to $250 or more, you need a written acknowledgment from that organization describing the services you provided and stating whether you received anything in return. A verbal thank-you at the annual gala doesn't cut it. Ask the nonprofit's treasurer or finance staff for a letter before tax season gets busy, not after.

Also confirm the organization qualifies. Not every cause you support is a registered 501(c)(3). The [IRS Charities & Nonprofits Resource Hub](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits) is the place to verify status before you count on a deduction that isn't there.

## Board service is common among our clients, and the rules apply the same way

A lot of the business owners we work with sit on boards: dentists on dental society committees, attorneys on legal aid boards, architects on design review panels for local nonprofits. The tax treatment doesn't change based on your profession or your billing rate. What changes is how much documentation discipline pays off, because professionals who track mileage and receipts carefully tend to be the ones who actually see a deduction when it's real.

If you're managing this alongside a business, the same habits that keep your company's expense tracking clean, one file per category, one log per vehicle, apply directly here. The volunteer expense rules aren't complicated once you separate "time" from "money spent," but the recordkeeping is where deductions get lost.

## Common Questions

**Can I deduct the value of professional services I donate for free?**
No. The IRS specifically disallows a deduction for the value of your time or services, regardless of your normal hourly rate. Only unreimbursed out-of-pocket costs directly connected to the volunteer work are deductible, per IRS Publication 526.

**What mileage rate do I use for volunteer driving?**
The charitable mileage rate is 14 cents per mile, a fixed statutory rate that hasn't changed since 1997. Alternatively, you can deduct actual gas and oil costs for the trips, but not depreciation, insurance, or repairs.

**Do I need a receipt for every small volunteer expense?**
You should keep records for everything, but a written acknowledgment from the organization becomes mandatory once your unreimbursed expenses for that organization total $250 or more in a year.

**Does it matter if the nonprofit is officially registered?**
Yes. Deductions only apply to contributions and expenses connected to a qualified organization. Verify status through the [IRS Charities & Nonprofits Resource Hub](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits) before assuming a deduction applies.

If you volunteer regularly, sit on a nonprofit board, or want to know how charitable giving fits into your broader tax picture as a business owner, [contact us](/contact) and we'll walk through what actually applies to your situation.

---


### Burnout Isn't a Business Strategy: Self-Care Belongs in Every Owner's Growth Plan
URL: /resources/burnout-isnt-a-business-strategy-self-care-should-be-part-of

A dentist in Hudson, Wisconsin, once told us he hadn't taken a real day off in three years. He wasn't bragging. He was explaining why his hygiene schedule was a mess, why he'd missed two insurance fee-schedule updates that cost him roughly $40,000 in underbilled claims, and why he kept putting off a conversation about hiring an associate. He wasn't lazy or careless. He was exhausted, and exhaustion had quietly become his business's biggest operating risk.

We've worked with business owners in Stillwater, Minnesota, and across the Twin Cities metro since 2005, and the pattern repeats across dentists, attorneys, architects, and service-based business owners alike: the owner who skips vacations and works through weekends isn't the most committed person in the room. They're often the one making the costliest decisions, because burnout doesn't announce itself. It shows up as a missed deadline, a bad hire, or a client contract signed without reading the fine print.

## Decision fatigue is a financial risk, not a mood

Every choice an owner makes draws from the same limited reserve of mental energy, whether it's picking a vendor, approving payroll, or deciding whether to take on a new client. Behavioral researchers call this decision fatigue, and it's well documented outside the business world too: judges granting parole are measurably more lenient right after a meal break than right before one. Tired brains default to the easiest choice, not the best one.

For a business owner, the easiest choice is usually to defer. Defer the collections call. Defer the rate increase. Defer the conversation about whether an employee is a fit. Each deferral feels harmless in the moment. Stacked over a fiscal year, they show up as thinner margins, slower accounts receivable, and a P&L that doesn't match the effort going into the business.

This isn't a productivity problem you fix with another app or a longer to-do list. It's a capacity problem, and capacity is a finite resource that has to be budgeted the same way cash is.

## The signs that show up in your books before they show up in your body

Owners often notice burnout in their mood or their sleep long after it has already started affecting the numbers. Here's what tends to surface first, and where:

| Warning sign | Where it shows up financially |
|---|---|
| Skipping monthly financial reviews | Cash flow surprises, missed KPI trends |
| Avoiding difficult client or vendor conversations | Aging receivables, scope creep on fixed-fee work |
| Delaying hiring decisions | Overtime costs, owner working below their billable rate |
| Ignoring subscription and expense creep | Recurring charges nobody remembers approving |
| Putting off retirement plan or benefits reviews | Missed employer match deadlines, lost tax deductions |

If even two of these describe the last quarter, the issue isn't a scheduling problem. It's a bandwidth problem, and bandwidth is what protects the judgment the business depends on.

## Rest belongs in the growth plan, not after it

Most owners treat rest as something they'll earn once the business is stable enough to afford it. That thinking has it backward. Stability comes from having enough reserve capacity, financial and mental, to handle the unexpected: a key employee quitting, a slow quarter, an IRS notice that needs a same-week response.

A sustainable operating rhythm looks a lot like a sustainable cash flow plan. You build in a buffer before you need it, not after. The [SBA's guidance on managing your business](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/manage-your-business) makes a similar point about ongoing operations: the businesses that last are the ones that plan for continuity, not just growth. That includes planning for the owner's own limits.

For the entrepreneurs and established small business owners we work with, that often means restructuring what actually requires the owner's attention. Weekly bookkeeping fires, payroll questions, and manual expense tracking eat hours that should go toward the decisions only the owner can make: pricing, hiring, and strategy. Handing off the operational load isn't giving something up. It's reallocating a limited resource toward the work that actually grows the business.

## What this looks like for a dental practice or a law firm

A solo attorney billing 2,200 hours a year and also doing her own bookkeeping on Sunday nights isn't more dedicated than one billing 1,900 hours with a quarterly financial review already scheduled. She's likely more profitable, because she's making pricing and staffing decisions with a clear head instead of a depleted one.

For dental practices, we see this most clearly around hygiene scheduling and fee reviews. An owner running four clinical days a week, doing payroll herself, and reviewing insurance write-offs at 9 p.m. is prone to exactly the kind of missed update that cost the Hudson dentist $40,000. Build in a standing quarterly review of production per hour, collection rate, and overhead percentage, and the owner sees the fee schedule issue in month one instead of month eleven. That's not a wellness fix. It's a reporting cadence that happens to protect both the owner's time and the practice's revenue.

The same logic applies to architects managing project overruns, insurance agencies tracking renewal commissions, and service-based businesses juggling irregular cash flow. The [entrepreneurs and established small business page](/industries/entrepreneurs-established-small-businesses) on our site covers how we build those recurring checkpoints, because the checkpoint itself is what gives an owner permission to step away without losing visibility.

## Building the habit, not just the intention

Self-care for a business owner rarely means a spa day. It means smaller, repeatable habits that reduce the number of decisions requiring full attention on any given day: a fixed time each week for financial review instead of constant checking, a delegated approval limit for routine expenses, and a real off switch on evenings when nothing is on fire. Our earlier piece on [building a healthier money mindset](/resources/quick-reads/5-tips-to-build-a-healthy-money-mindset-and-grow-your-finances) walks through habits in the same spirit, aimed at reducing financial anxiety before it becomes financial paralysis.

Owners who build these habits early tend to make fewer reactive decisions later, whether that's a rushed hire, an underpriced contract, or a missed retirement plan contribution deadline. The habit isn't glamorous. It's a recurring calendar block that protects judgment the same way a cash reserve protects solvency.

## Common Questions

**Is self-care really a financial issue, or is this just a wellness trend applied to business advice?**
It's financial in a direct sense: exhausted owners make measurably worse decisions, from missed fee updates to delayed hiring, and those decisions show up on the P&L. Treating rest as part of the operating plan is a risk-management choice, not a lifestyle preference.

**How much rest does a business owner actually need to protect decision-making?**
There's no universal number, but the pattern we see across dentists, attorneys, and service-business owners is consistent: owners who protect at least one full day a week away from operational decisions, plus a real vacation stretch each year, catch financial issues (fee schedules, aging receivables, subscription creep) months earlier than owners who don't.

**What's the first practical step toward reducing owner burnout without hurting revenue?**
Start with a recurring financial review, weekly or monthly, that's scheduled rather than reactive. Owners who see cash flow and KPI trends on a fixed cadence make fewer emergency decisions, which is often what's driving the exhaustion in the first place.

**Can outsourcing accounting and payroll actually reduce burnout?**
Yes, for many owners it's the single biggest time and mental-load reduction available, because it removes the daily and weekly financial tasks that otherwise compete with strategic decisions. It doesn't remove ownership of the numbers, it removes the manual burden of producing them.

If your own schedule looks like the one described here, four clinical or billable days, evenings spent on bookkeeping, and no real review of where the money is going, it's worth a conversation before the next fee schedule or missed deadline makes the decision for you. [Contact us](/contact) to talk through what a sustainable financial rhythm could look like for your practice or business.

### How to Turn a Second Home Into a Tax Win
URL: /resources/how-to-turn-a-second-home-into-a-tax-win

A cabin on a Wisconsin lake or a condo near the Gulf changes more than your weekend plans. It changes how the IRS looks at your tax return, and the difference comes down to one number: how many days a year you rent the place out versus use it yourself. Cross that line and a relaxing getaway turns into a rental business with its own reporting rules, deduction limits, and record-keeping demands. Stay under it and you keep the simpler tax treatment of a personal residence, mortgage interest deduction included.

Most of what shows up when you search for second home tax advice comes from real estate agents talking about square footage and resale value. That's useful for the purchase decision, but it skips the part that actually determines your tax bill: the IRS doesn't care what you call the property. It cares how you use it.

## The 14-day rule that decides your tax treatment

If you rent the property for 14 days or fewer during the tax year, you don't report the rental income at all, regardless of how much you collected. You can still deduct mortgage interest and property taxes as itemized deductions, the same way you would for your primary home. This is the rule that lets someone rent their lake place for the Fourth of July week or a hunting opener weekend without touching a Schedule E.

Cross 14 rental days and the income becomes reportable. From there, the IRS splits your expenses between personal use and rental use based on the number of days each applies, and how much you can deduct depends on how the property gets classified. [IRS Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527) walks through the mechanics in detail, and [IRS Tax Topic 415](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc415) covers the reporting basics for rental and vacation property.

## Personal use vs. rental use: how the days actually get counted

This is where most owners miscount without realizing it. A day counts as personal use if:

- You or a family member stays there, even if you pay fair rental price
- You let someone stay there for free or at a reduced rate
- You swap use of the home with another owner under a reciprocal arrangement

A day does not count as personal use if you're there mainly to perform repairs or maintenance, and that distinction matters more than it sounds. An owner who spends a weekend replacing a dock or repainting a bedroom can document that as maintenance time rather than personal use, which shifts the ratio in their favor.

Once personal use exceeds the greater of 14 days or 10% of the days the home was rented at fair value, the IRS treats the property as a personal residence with rental activity attached. That triggers a specific limitation: your rental deductions can't exceed your rental income. No loss carries over to offset your W-2 or business income that year, though unused expenses generally carry forward.

## Second home vs. investment property: what changes on your return

The label you put on the property doesn't matter to the IRS. The use pattern does. Here's how the three common scenarios play out:

| Use pattern | Reporting | Deduction limits |
|---|---|---|
| Rented 14 days or fewer per year | No rental income reported | Mortgage interest and property tax deductible on Schedule A |
| Personal use exceeds 14 days or 10% of rental days | Rental income reported on Schedule E | Expenses limited to rental income; no loss allowed |
| Personal use stays under the 14-day/10% threshold | Rental income reported on Schedule E | Full expenses and depreciation allowed; losses may be deductible up to $25,000 if you actively participate, subject to income phase-outs between $100,000 and $150,000 AGI |

That third row is the one people searching "second home vs investment property" are usually trying to reach. It requires keeping personal use genuinely minimal, which for a family cabin is harder than it sounds. A long Fourth of July stay, a few weekends in the fall, and a week at Christmas can eat through 14 days before Labor Day.

## What you can deduct once rental income applies

Once the property crosses into rental territory, the expense list expands considerably: mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, utilities, cleaning and maintenance, association dues, and depreciation on the structure itself. Each of these gets allocated between personal and rental days based on total days used during the year. Days the home sat vacant generally don't count toward either side of that ratio, which surprises owners who assume an empty week adds to their personal-use column.

Depreciation is the deduction most owners underuse. A rental home's structure (not the land) gets depreciated over 27.5 years under IRS rules, and that deduction reduces taxable rental income even in years the property throws off positive cash flow. It also creates depreciation recapture exposure at sale, which is worth planning around well before you list the property.

## A lake cabin example from Wisconsin

Consider a business owner client who buys a cabin near Hayward, Wisconsin. They use it 20 days a year themselves and rent it out through a platform for 40 days at market rate. Personal use of 20 days exceeds the greater of 14 days or 10% of 40 rental days (4 days), so the property falls into the limited-deduction category: rental expenses can offset rental income, but any excess doesn't create a deductible loss that year.

Now change the numbers. The same client cuts personal use to 12 days and rents the cabin 60 days a year. Personal use now falls under the 14-day threshold, which opens the door to full expense deductions, depreciation, and a potential loss deduction against other income, subject to the $100,000 to $150,000 AGI phase-out for active participation. Twelve days of difference in usage changes the entire tax posture of the property.

That's the calculation worth running before you decide how often to block off the calendar for personal use, and it's a different conversation than the one a realtor or property manager will have with you.

## Where this intersects with your broader financial picture

A second home rarely sits in isolation from the rest of a client's finances. Business owners buying a cabin or vacation condo are often the same clients managing cash flow, evaluating retirement contributions, and coordinating with a financial advisor on where extra income should go. The rental-day math above is straightforward once you track it, but the harder question is usually whether the property fits the rest of the budget, and whether the tax benefit is worth the trade-off in flexibility. If you're weighing a purchase at all, [our breakdown of buying versus renting](/resources/do-the-math-behind-renting-vs-buying-a-home) covers the cash flow side of that decision.

For business owners already juggling entity structure and quarterly estimates, a rental property adds another layer of recordkeeping. It's worth folding into the same planning conversation covered in [our piece on getting ahead of higher taxes](/resources/quick-reads/4-steps-to-get-ahead-of-higher-taxes), since the timing of income and deductions from a vacation rental can shift your estimated payment calculations mid-year.

## Common Questions

**What is the IRS 14-day rule for a second home?**
If you rent your second home for 14 days or fewer during the tax year, you don't report that rental income on your return, no matter the amount collected, and you keep the standard mortgage interest and property tax deductions available to any personal residence.

**Is renting out my vacation home considered a business?**
Not automatically. It becomes a reportable rental activity once you exceed 14 rental days, but whether losses are deductible depends on your personal-use days relative to rental days, tracked under the rules in [IRS Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527).

**Should I buy a second home as an investment property instead of a personal one?**
That depends on how you plan to use it. Treating it as an investment property with minimal personal use (under 14 days or 10% of rental days) opens up full deductions and depreciation, but it also means genuinely limiting your own time there, which many owners find harder in practice than on paper.

**Do I need to report rental income if I only rent a few weekends a year?**
If total rental days stay at 14 or fewer for the year, no. Once you exceed 14 days, all of that rental income becomes reportable, even the portion collected during those first 14 days.

If you're weighing a second home purchase, already renting one out, or trying to sort out which side of the 14-day line you landed on last year, a conversation before you file beats guessing after. [Contact us](/contact) to talk through the numbers with a CPA who works with business owners and property owners across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and nationwide.

---


### Long-Term Care: How You Can Financially Prepare for the Expense
URL: /resources/long-term-care-how-you-can-financially-prepare-for-the-expen

A long-term care event doesn't send a warning text three years ahead of time. It shows up as a fall, a diagnosis, or a spouse who can no longer manage alone, and suddenly a family is choosing a memory care facility on a Tuesday afternoon with no plan for how to pay for it. We work with business owners, dentists, and attorneys across Minnesota and Wisconsin who have built substantial retirement accounts and real estate equity, and most of them have never run the numbers on what a two-year stay in assisted living would do to that plan. This isn't a topic to solve in a crisis. It's a funding decision, and like any funding decision, it works better when it's made years in advance with real numbers instead of guesses.

## What long-term care actually costs

In Minnesota and Wisconsin, a private room in a nursing home commonly runs $90,000 to $120,000 a year, depending on the facility and location. Assisted living tends to fall in the $50,000 to $65,000 range annually, and a home health aide working 40 hours a week can add up to $50,000 or more a year once you account for overtime and holiday rates. None of these numbers include the cost of home modifications, medical equipment, or the informal caregiving that adult children often absorb by cutting back their own work hours.

The average nursing home stay is a little over two years, but a meaningful share of people need care for five years or longer, particularly with dementia-related conditions. Run the low end and the high end side by side and the swing is enormous: $180,000 versus $600,000 or more for the same category of care, depending entirely on how long someone needs it. That range is exactly why long-term care planning has to be treated as risk management, not budgeting.

## Three ways to fund the risk

Most families end up paying for long-term care through some combination of three sources: long-term care insurance, government benefits (primarily Medicaid and, for veterans, VA Aid and Attendance), and personal savings. Medicare covers very little of this. It pays for short-term skilled nursing after a hospital stay, generally capped around 100 days, and stops well short of the custodial care that makes up most long-term care needs. That gap is where planning either pays off or doesn't.

| Funding source | What it covers | Who it fits |
|---|---|---|
| Long-term care insurance | Daily or monthly benefit for home care, assisted living, or nursing home care, usually with a benefit period and elimination period | Clients in their 50s to mid-60s who are still insurable and want to cap their exposure |
| VA Aid and Attendance | Monthly cash benefit added to a veteran's pension for those who need help with daily activities | Wartime veterans and surviving spouses who meet service and income/asset tests |
| Self-funding from savings | Retirement accounts, brokerage assets, home equity, or cash reserves earmarked for care | Clients with $2 million or more in liquid net worth who can absorb the cost without insurance |

## Long-term care insurance vs self-funding

Long-term care insurance makes the most sense for people who have significant assets to protect but not so much that a five-year, $600,000 care event is a rounding error. A typical policy purchased in your late 50s might run $2,500 to $4,000 a year in premium for a benefit that covers $150,000 to $250,000 of care costs, adjusted for inflation riders. The math works because you're transferring a large, uncertain cost onto an insurer for a smaller, known one, the same logic behind any insurance purchase. We walk through this the same way we help clients size other coverage, which is the subject of our piece on [how much insurance coverage you actually need](/resources/insuring-where-it-counts-avoid-over-insuring-in-the-wrong-pl-2).

Self-funding is the right call for a smaller group of clients, generally those with $2 million-plus in investable assets who can treat a care event as a large but survivable draw on the portfolio. Even then, self-funding works best when it's a deliberate decision, with a specific pool of assets earmarked and the withdrawal strategy coordinated with a financial advisor rather than pulled ad hoc from whatever account is easiest to liquidate. This is one of the areas where we sit down with a client's financial advisor directly, because the sequencing of withdrawals, the tax bracket impact, and the timing around required minimum distributions all interact with a care-cost decision. It also ties back to how the underlying portfolio is built to weather that kind of draw, which is why the discipline around [why a balanced portfolio isn't a set-it-and-forget-it decision](/resources/strategically-balancing-your-investment-portfolio-why-set-it) matters here too.

Most families land somewhere in between: a smaller insurance policy that caps the worst-case scenario, backed by a savings cushion for anything the policy doesn't cover. There's no single right answer, but there is a wrong one, which is deciding nothing and hoping Medicaid or a family member fills the gap.

## Veterans benefits many families miss

Wartime veterans and their surviving spouses may qualify for the VA's Aid and Attendance benefit, a monthly payment added on top of a standard VA pension for those who need help with daily activities like bathing, dressing, or managing medication. The benefit is meaningful, often several hundred to over a thousand dollars a month depending on the household, but it comes with service, income, and net worth requirements that trip up a lot of otherwise-eligible families. Full details on eligibility and the application process are on the VA's own [Aid and Attendance and Housebound benefits page](https://www.va.gov/pension/aid-attendance-housebound/).

We see this benefit get overlooked constantly, particularly among clients who assume their income is too high to qualify without checking the actual thresholds, or who don't realize unreimbursed medical and care expenses can be deducted when calculating countable income. If there's a veteran or a veteran's surviving spouse anywhere in the family who might need care in the next few years, it's worth confirming eligibility before assuming the benefit doesn't apply.

## Tax treatment of long-term care costs

Long-term care insurance premiums and unreimbursed long-term care expenses can qualify as deductible medical expenses, subject to the usual 7.5%-of-AGI floor for itemized medical deductions, and premium deductibility is further capped by age-based limits that adjust annually. Qualified long-term care services themselves, along with premiums for tax-qualified policies, are addressed directly in [IRS Publication 502 on medical and dental expenses](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502), which is the reference we use when we're building this into a client's tax projection. For business owners, there's also a separate conversation about whether a C-corporation or certain pass-through structures can deduct LTC premiums as a business expense on behalf of an owner-employee, which is worth reviewing with your entity structure in mind rather than assuming one rule fits every client.

## Building long-term care into your broader plan

The clients who handle this well aren't necessarily the wealthiest ones. They're the ones who treat long-term care as a line item in retirement planning the same way they treat a mortgage payoff date or a business succession timeline: something with a number attached, reviewed periodically, and coordinated across the people advising them. For a business owner or dentist in their late 50s, that usually means three conversations happening together instead of separately: what the practice or business is worth and when it might be sold, what the retirement portfolio can realistically absorb, and whether insurance makes sense to buy now while health still allows for affordable underwriting. We coordinate the tax and cash flow side of that conversation and loop in a client's financial advisor for the insurance and investment side, which tends to produce a plan that actually gets funded instead of one that sits in a drawer.

## Common Questions

**How much does long-term care insurance typically cost?**
Premiums vary by age, health, and benefit design, but a policy purchased in your late 50s with a moderate daily benefit and inflation protection commonly runs $2,500 to $4,000 a year. Buying earlier, while you're healthier, generally locks in a lower premium than waiting until your late 60s.

**Does Medicare pay for nursing home care?**
Medicare covers only short-term skilled nursing care following a qualifying hospital stay, typically capped around 100 days, and it does not cover the ongoing custodial care that makes up most long-term care needs. That gap is precisely why insurance, VA benefits, or savings need to be lined up separately.

**Can veterans get help paying for assisted living?**
Wartime veterans and surviving spouses who meet service, income, and net worth requirements may qualify for the VA's Aid and Attendance benefit, a monthly payment that can be applied toward home care, assisted living, or nursing home costs. Details on eligibility are on the VA's Aid and Attendance and Housebound benefits page.

**Are long-term care insurance premiums tax deductible?**
Premiums for a tax-qualified long-term care policy can count as a deductible medical expense, subject to age-based dollar limits and the 7.5%-of-AGI threshold for itemized medical deductions, as outlined in IRS Publication 502.

If you're weighing insurance, VA benefits, and savings against each other and want the numbers run against your actual retirement accounts and business structure, [contact us](/contact) and we'll walk through what funding mix fits your situation.

---


### Insuring Where It Counts: How Much Insurance Coverage Do You Actually Need
URL: /resources/insuring-where-it-counts-avoid-over-insuring-in-the-wrong-pl-2

A dentist in Stillwater called us last year holding two life insurance policies, a disability policy she'd forgotten she was paying for, and an umbrella policy sized for a net worth she'd outgrown a decade ago. She was paying roughly $4,200 a year for coverage that didn't match her actual exposure. Meanwhile, her practice, which represented most of her net worth, carried no business interruption coverage at all. That's the pattern we see constantly: too much insurance in low-risk corners, not enough where a single event could wipe out years of savings.

Most insurance advice treats coverage like a shopping list: get life insurance, get disability, get an umbrella policy, check the boxes. That approach misses the actual question, which is a math problem, not a checklist item. How much would a specific loss cost you, and how much of that cost can your cash flow or net worth absorb without insurance? Everything above that line is what you insure. Everything below it, you're often paying to insure twice.

## Insurance is a math problem before it's a shopping list

Every insurance decision comes down to two numbers: the probability of a loss and the severity if it happens. A $30,000 loss that you could cover from savings without much disruption doesn't need a policy built around it. A $2 million loss that would end your business or your family's financial security does. The confusion happens when people insure against probability (how likely something feels) instead of severity (how much it would actually cost).

Take two business owners with identical annual revenue of $800,000. One runs a service-based consulting firm with no inventory, no real estate, and low liability exposure. The other owns a dental practice with $650,000 in equipment, a build-out lease, and patient risk exposure that never fully goes away. Both might feel the same size on a P&L, but their insurance needs analysis produces completely different numbers. Sizing coverage off revenue or gut feeling, rather than actual exposure, is how the first owner ends up over-insured and the second ends up dangerously exposed.

## Personal coverage sized against net worth, not a rule of thumb

The old formula, "buy 10 times your income in life insurance," ignores what you're actually trying to protect. The real question is: if you died tomorrow, what dollar amount would your dependents need to replace lost income and pay off debt, and how much of that gap does your current net worth already cover?

Here's how that plays out for a business owner with $900,000 in net worth, including $500,000 in home equity and a business interest, two kids, and a spouse earning $70,000 a year. If the family needs $90,000 a year in income for 15 years until the kids are independent, that's roughly $1.35 million in income replacement need. Subtract the spouse's earning capacity and liquid net worth, and the actual gap might land closer to $700,000 to $900,000 in term life coverage, not the $1.5 million a generic multiplier would suggest.

Umbrella liability works the same way. If your net worth is $1.2 million and your auto policy caps out at $300,000 in liability, you have an $900,000 hole that a single serious accident could expose. A $1 million umbrella policy, layered on top of standard auto and homeowners liability limits, usually costs $200 to $400 a year for that protection. That's cheap relative to the exposure it closes.

Disability insurance deserves the same scrutiny, especially for dentists, attorneys, and other professionals whose income depends entirely on their ability to work. A dentist earning $250,000 a year who becomes unable to practice isn't facing a temporary setback; they're facing the loss of their primary asset. Own-occupation disability coverage, not the cheaper any-occupation version, is usually the right fit here, and it's a conversation worth having alongside whoever manages your investment accounts, not in isolation.

## Business coverage tied to what would actually sink you

On the business side, the risk-based approach applies with even more force, because business losses hit cash flow directly and immediately. A useful business insurance coverage checklist starts with naming the specific exposure, not the policy type.

| Exposure | Coverage type | Who it matters most for |
|---|---|---|
| Physical damage to property or equipment | Commercial property insurance | Dentists, specialty healthcare practices with fixed equipment |
| Lawsuit from a client, patient, or third party | General liability | Service-based businesses, architects |
| Errors in professional advice or work product | Professional liability (E&O) | Attorneys, architects, insurance agencies |
| Forced closure from fire, storm, or covered event | Business interruption | Any business with a physical location |
| Data breach or ransomware event | Cyber liability | Firms handling client financial or health data |
| Loss of a key owner or partner | Key person life insurance | Firms with 1-3 owners generating most of the revenue |

The mistake we see most often isn't skipping a category entirely; it's buying the cheapest version of coverage in every category instead of the right depth in the two or three that matter most. A law firm with minimal physical inventory doesn't need aggressive property coverage, but it absolutely needs professional liability limits that match its largest historical client engagements. An architecture firm facing a lawsuit over a design defect years after project completion needs coverage that extends past the policy period, not just during it.

Business insurance premiums are generally deductible as an ordinary business expense, with specifics laid out in [IRS Publication 535](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p535). That deductibility doesn't change the sizing decision, but it does mean the after-tax cost of adequate coverage is lower than the sticker price suggests, which shifts the math in favor of closing real gaps rather than trimming premiums at the margins.

## A needs analysis you can run in twenty minutes

A proper insurance needs analysis doesn't require an actuary. It requires four steps, done honestly:

1. List every asset and income stream exposed to loss: your practice, your home, your investment accounts, your earning capacity.
2. Estimate the maximum realistic loss for each, not the average case. What would a total loss actually cost?
3. Subtract what your cash reserves, emergency fund, or net worth could absorb without insurance.
4. Insure the remaining gap, and only that gap, with the right policy type.

Run that exercise once a year, or whenever a major change hits: a new building lease, a second location, a child born, a spouse leaving the workforce. Coverage that fit two years ago doesn't automatically fit today. Business owners we work with through [outsourced accounting](/industries/entrepreneurs-established-small-businesses) engagements tend to revisit this alongside their annual budget and KPI review, because the same cash flow numbers that drive a budget also drive an accurate needs analysis.

## Where over-insuring quietly drains cash flow

Over-insurance rarely looks dramatic. It shows up as small, recurring charges that add up: a rider on a homeowners policy covering jewelry you don't own anymore, duplicate accidental death coverage bundled into three different accounts, an extended warranty on a business vehicle that's already covered under a commercial auto policy. None of these individually breaks a budget. Together, they behave like the recurring charges we've written about in [subscription creep](/resources/take-back-control-of-subscription-creep): small, invisible, and steadily pulling cash away from goals that matter more.

Whole life insurance sold as a retirement vehicle is the biggest one we flag for business owners in their 30s and 40s. If the goal is death benefit protection, term insurance covering the actual income-replacement gap, paired with the premium difference invested separately, usually outperforms whole life on both cost and flexibility. Whole life has a place for specific estate planning or business succession situations, particularly for owners funding a buy-sell agreement, but it's frequently sold as a default rather than a fit.

On the business side, we've reviewed policies for insurance agency clients and specialty healthcare practices carrying overlapping general liability and umbrella coverage that duplicated limits already sitting in a professional liability policy. Every dollar spent on redundant coverage is a dollar not going toward retirement plan contributions, equipment upgrades, or the cash reserve that actually protects the business during a slow quarter, a point we've also raised in looking at [why small businesses go bankrupt despite steady sales](/resources/quick-reads/why-small-businesses-are-going-bankrupt-and-how-to-avoid-it).

## Common Questions

**How much life insurance coverage do I actually need?**
Calculate the income your dependents would need annually, multiply by the number of years until they're financially independent, then subtract your liquid net worth and any spouse income. The remainder is your term life coverage target, not a flat multiple of your salary.

**Do I need an umbrella policy if I already have auto and home insurance?**
If your net worth exceeds your auto and homeowners liability limits combined, yes. A $1 million umbrella policy typically runs a few hundred dollars a year and closes a gap that a single lawsuit could otherwise expose in full.

**Are business insurance premiums tax deductible?**
Generally yes, as an ordinary and necessary business expense. [IRS Publication 535](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p535) outlines which premiums qualify and where the exceptions apply, particularly around life insurance where the business is the beneficiary.

**How often should I redo my insurance needs analysis?**
At minimum once a year, and immediately after any major change: a new lease, a second location, a child, a spouse's job change, or a significant jump in net worth. Coverage sized for last year's numbers rarely fits this year's exposure.

If you want a second set of eyes on where your coverage actually sits against your net worth and cash flow, or you're trying to figure out whether your business's policies overlap with your personal ones, [contact us](/contact) and we'll walk through the numbers with you.

---


### Insuring Where It Counts: How Much Insurance Coverage Do You Actually Need
URL: /resources/insuring-where-it-counts-avoid-over-insuring-in-the-wrong-pl

Ask ten people how much insurance they need and you'll get ten different lists: life insurance, disability, umbrella, general liability, cyber, key person. What you won't get is math. Insurance coverage isn't a shopping list, it's a risk-based calculation that starts with two numbers: what you're worth and what you'd lose if a specific bad event happened next Tuesday. Get those numbers right and the right coverage amounts fall out of the calculation. Skip them and you end up over-insured in places that don't matter and dangerously exposed in the ones that do.

We see this pattern constantly with dentists, attorneys, architects, and service-business owners across Minnesota and Wisconsin. A dental practice owner carries a disability policy sized for a solo associate's income from ten years ago, while the practice itself has no buy-sell funding if a partner becomes permanently disabled. An insurance agency owner has excellent E&O coverage but no plan for what happens to cash flow if a key producer leaves with half the book. The policies exist. They're just aimed at the wrong risks.

## The real question is what you can absorb, not what you can buy

Every insurance decision is really a decision about who absorbs a loss: you, your business, or the insurer. If you have $400,000 in liquid net worth and a lawsuit exposure that could realistically reach $2 million, that gap is what needs coverage. If your business could survive a $15,000 equipment loss out of cash reserves without blinking, insuring that risk with a low deductible is money spent on a problem you could already solve yourself.

This is the piece most insurance conversations skip. Agents sell products. A needs analysis starts from your balance sheet and asks what dollar amount of loss would actually change your financial position, then works backward to a coverage number. The IRS treats most business insurance premiums as deductible under [IRS Publication 535](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p535), which is useful to know, but deductibility shouldn't be the reason you buy a policy. Exposure should be.

## Start with your balance sheet, not a stack of policies

A personal risk management plan begins with three figures: net worth, annual cash flow needs, and the dollar value of what would be catastrophic to lose. For a 45-year-old architect with $900,000 in retirement accounts, a paid-down home, and two kids approaching college, the catastrophic risks are usually disability income and liability from a professional errors claim, not a large term life policy that was sized when the mortgage was bigger and the kids were toddlers.

Run the numbers instead of guessing. A rough framework:

| Risk category | Question to answer | What sizes the coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Life insurance | What income or debt obligation disappears if you die? | Outstanding debt plus years of replacement income needed, minus existing assets |
| Disability income | How long could you cover expenses with savings alone? | Monthly fixed expenses times months of reserve gap |
| Umbrella liability | What single event could exceed your auto or homeowner's limits? | Net worth exposed to a lawsuit above underlying policy limits |
| Business liability | What claim would exceed what the business could pay from operating cash? | Realistic claim size minus cash reserves and existing coverage |

Most people who feel "under-insured" have never actually run this table. They've bought whatever an agent recommended at a life event, life insurance at the mortgage closing, disability through an employer's default election, and never revisited it against current net worth. Net worth changes every year. Coverage rarely gets adjusted to match it.

## How business owners should size coverage against what the business can't survive without

For a service-based business or a specialty healthcare practice, the calculation shifts from personal net worth to operating cash flow and key-person risk. Ask three questions before renewing any commercial policy:

First, what single event would force the business to stop operating for more than 30 days? For a dental or specialty healthcare practice, that's usually a facility loss or a sudden absence of the primary provider, not a slip-and-fall claim already covered under general liability. Business interruption and key person coverage matter more here than an extra layer of umbrella limits.

Second, what claim size is realistic for your field? An architecture firm's professional liability exposure looks different from a law firm's, which looks different from an insurance agency's E&O risk. Pulling three years of industry claims data, something your liability carrier can usually provide, gives you a defensible number instead of a guess. Buying limits well beyond that realistic range is paying premium dollars for a risk that's already vanishingly small.

Third, what would happen to cash flow if a partner or key employee left tomorrow? This is where a lot of small businesses are quietly under-insured. A firm generating $1.8 million in revenue with two equal partners and no buy-sell funding is one health event away from a forced, undercapitalized buyout. That's a bigger threat to the business than most of the property coverage owners spend time optimizing. If cash flow pressure is already a concern in your business, this [breakdown of why profitable small businesses still fail](/resources/quick-reads/why-small-businesses-are-going-bankrupt-and-how-to-avoid-it) covers the same root issue from a different angle.

## Where over-insuring quietly drains cash flow

Over-insurance rarely looks dramatic. It looks like a $2,000-deductible policy where a $10,000 deductible would cut the premium by 20% and the business has enough reserve to absorb the difference. It looks like a term life policy carried past the point where the mortgage is paid off and the kids are financially independent. It looks like duplicate coverage: a personal umbrella policy and a business policy both covering the same liability exposure because nobody compared the two documents side by side.

Each of these costs real money every year, money that could go toward retirement contributions, debt paydown, or reinvestment in the practice. A dentist paying $380 a month for disability coverage sized to a $220,000 income from 2015, when current income is $310,000 and savings have grown substantially, is both under-insured on the income gap and over-insured relative to what a properly structured policy would cost for the right benefit amount. The fix isn't more insurance. It's a recalculation.

## A simple exposure exercise you can run this week

Pull three documents: your most recent personal financial statement, your business balance sheet, and your current insurance declarations pages. For each policy, write down the coverage limit and then write down, honestly, the dollar loss that would actually hurt. If the limit is far above the realistic loss, you're likely over-insured there. If it's below, that's the gap to close first.

This exercise works the same way portfolio rebalancing does: risk exposure shifts as your net worth and life circumstances change, so a static coverage plan calcifies into either overpayment or a dangerous gap. The same logic behind [why a balanced investment portfolio isn't a set-it-and-forget-it decision](/resources/strategically-balancing-your-investment-portfolio-why-set-it) applies directly to insurance. Net worth grows, debt gets paid down, kids graduate, practices expand. Coverage should move with those changes, not sit frozen at whatever level made sense five years ago.

We work through this exercise regularly with dentists and specialty healthcare practices whose personal and business risk profiles are tightly linked, since a practice owner's income, the practice's cash flow, and personal net worth often rise and fall together. If you're in that position, our [industry page for dental practices](/industries/dentists) outlines how we coordinate that kind of planning alongside tax and cash flow work. The same approach applies to entrepreneurs and established small businesses more broadly, covered on our [entrepreneurs and small business page](/industries/entrepreneurs-established-small-businesses).

## Common Questions

**How much insurance coverage do I actually need?**
The amount depends on the gap between your net worth and your realistic loss exposure in each category: life, disability, liability, and property. There's no universal number. A useful starting point is calculating what dollar loss in each category would force a change in your lifestyle or business operations, then sizing coverage to close that specific gap rather than following a generic rule of thumb like "ten times income."

**What's the difference between personal and business insurance needs analysis?**
A personal analysis starts with net worth, dependents, and income replacement needs. A business analysis starts with operating cash flow, key-person dependency, and realistic claim sizes for your industry. Business owners usually need both run side by side, since a personal financial shock and a business one often hit at the same time.

**Is business insurance tax deductible?**
Most ordinary business insurance premiums, including liability, property, and business interruption coverage, are deductible as a business expense under [IRS Publication 535](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p535). Deductibility isn't a reason to buy more coverage than your exposure warrants, but it does affect the after-tax cost of the coverage you actually need.

**How often should I revisit my coverage amounts?**
At minimum, revisit coverage after any major shift: a new partner, a change in revenue, a paid-off mortgage, or a change in net worth of 20% or more in either direction. Absent a major event, an annual review alongside tax planning catches most drift before it becomes a real gap or a wasted premium.

If your coverage hasn't been checked against your current net worth and cash flow in a while, that's worth fixing before it costs you either an unnecessary premium or a real gap. [Contact us](/contact) to set up a risk review alongside your tax and cash flow planning.
